extracted.intended_audience: editors, authors, copyeditors, and publishers using Chicago style
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines from The Chicago Manual of Style on how to format, punctuate, and capitalize names, terms, and titles of works and how to handle numerals versus spelled-out numbers in running text, notes, and bibliographies. Covers many specific classes of works (books, periodicals, poems, films, websites, music, etc.) and rules for numerals, ordinals, large numbers, and scientific notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing subtitle by typeface or punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: A subtitle is often distinguished from a title by a different typeface; when referred to it is separated from the title by a colon. When an em dash rather than a colon is used, what follows the em dash is not normally considered to be a subtitle, and the first word is not necessarily capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If title and subtitle on a title page are distinguished by typeface alone, add a colon when referring to the full title. A dash in the original should be retained; a semicolon between title and subtitle may usually be changed to a colon. See examples and 14.90, 14.97 for exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve original spelling and hyphenation of titles
rubrics_metrics.description: When a title is referred to in text, notes, or bibliographies, its original spelling (including non-Latin letters) and hyphenation should be preserved, regardless of the style used in surrounding text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalization may be changed to headline or sentence style. As editorial discretion, ampersand may be changed to 'and' and numerals sometimes spelled out (see 14.88). Add commas omitted at ends of title lines; add serial commas only if clear they are used in the work itself (see 6.19).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of titles: headline vs sentence style
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalization of referred titles may be changed to headline style (8.159) or sentence style (8.158), as applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the chosen capitalization consistently; see chapter references for detailed headline/sentence capitalization rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma and punctuation restoration in referred titles
rubrics_metrics.description: On title pages, commas are sometimes omitted from line ends; when such a title is referred to, such commas should be added, including any comma omitted before a date that appears on a line by itself at the end of a title or subtitle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serial commas should be added only if it is clear they are used in the work itself. Restore punctuation that was omitted for aesthetic line breaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles take singular verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: A title, considered a singular noun, always takes a singular verb, even if the title is plural in form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let punctuation or plural-looking titles change verb agreement: e.g., 'The Waves is not a typical novel.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation in a title does not affect surrounding text
rubrics_metrics.description: Any punctuation that is part of a title should not affect the punctuation of the surrounding text (except that a sentence-ending period is omitted after a title ending in a question mark or exclamation point).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: use commas or punctuation of the surrounding sentence as if the title's internal punctuation were not present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double titles connected by 'or' — prefer original punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: For old-fashioned double titles connected by 'or' prefer the punctuation on the title page or the original source; if unavailable, prefer the simpler form shown in examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This favors editorial expediency while balancing fidelity to originals. See examples: 'The Tempest, or The Enchanted Island' vs 'Moby-Dick; or, The Whale'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Books and periodical titles: italics and headline capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: When mentioned in text, notes, or bibliography, titles and subtitles of books and periodicals are italicized and capitalized headline-style (though some publications may require sentence style in reference lists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A full book title cited in notes/bibliography may be shortened in text; see 14.30 for short-title notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial articles in book titles may be dropped in running text
rubrics_metrics.description: An initial 'a,' 'an,' or 'the' in book titles may be dropped from running text if it does not fit the surrounding syntax; retain it when in doubt or when indispensable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Fielding, in his introduction to The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling...' vs 'Fielding’s History of Tom Jones...'. Maintain readability and syntax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial 'the' in periodical titles is usually lowercased in running text
rubrics_metrics.description: When newspapers and other periodicals are mentioned in running text, an initial 'the' (even if part of the masthead) is usually lowercased (unless it begins a sentence) and not italicized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many periodicals are referred to with a definite article; treating it as part of surrounding text facilitates consistent discussion. Some editors may prefer retaining an initial 'The' with single-word periodical titles; use consistently and only when article is actually part of the title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain non-English article only if official part of title
rubrics_metrics.description: Because it may govern inflection, non-English titles retain the article in the original language—but only if it is an official part of the title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'We read Le Monde and Die Zeit' but 'Did you see the review in the Frankfurter Allgemeine?'. In citation form initial 'the' is dropped from periodical titles except where incorporated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive words like 'magazine' italicized only if part of official title
rubrics_metrics.description: A word like magazine, journal, or review should be italicized only when it forms part of the official title of a particular periodical; when functioning as a descriptive term it is part of surrounding text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'I read it both in Time magazine and in the Wall Street Journal' vs 'His article was reprinted in the New York Times Magazine.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodical titles used as part of names (buildings, prizes) are not italicized
rubrics_metrics.description: When the title of a newspaper or periodical is part of the name of a building, organization, prize, or the like, it is not italicized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Los Angeles Times Book Prize | Chicago Defender Charities Tribune Tower'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse italics: terms that would be italicized within an italicized title set in roman
rubrics_metrics.description: Any term within an italicized title that itself would be italicized in running text—such as a foreign word, a genus name, or the name of a ship—should be set in roman type (reverse italics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'From Tyrannosaurus rex to King Kong: Large Creatures in Fact and Fiction' and 'The Big E: The Story of the USS Enterprise'.

rubrics_metrics.name: A title of a work within another title remains italicized and receives quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: A title of a work within another title should remain in italics and be enclosed in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'A Key to Whitehead’s “Process and Reality”'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use a title to stand for the subject of a work
rubrics_metrics.description: The title of a work should not be used to stand for the subject of the work; use phrasing that indicates discussion of subject rather than the title itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Dostoevsky wrote a book about crime and punishment (not... about Crime and Punishment).'

rubrics_metrics.name: Multivolume works treated like single-volume works
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of multivolume books and named titles of individual volumes are treated the same as single-volume works; the word 'volume' may be abbreviated parenthetically and is capitalized only if part of the title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For bibliographic treatment of multivolume works see 14.116-22; examples given for referencing volumes and special cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles of series and editions: capitalization but no italics
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of book series and editions are capitalized but not italicized. The words 'series' and 'edition' are capitalized only if part of the title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numbered or named editions of a specific publication usually are not part of the title and are set in roman and lowercase; consult library catalog when in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articles, chapters, and parts: roman type and quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of articles and features in periodicals, chapter and part titles, titles of short stories or essays, and individual selections in books are set in roman type and enclosed in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Book titles and normally italicized terms inside article titles remain italicized; terms quoted in original title are in single quotation marks inside double quotation marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collected works: include originally separate books in italics
rubrics_metrics.description: When two or more works originally published as separate books are included in a single volume (collected works), they are best italicized rather than put in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The introduction to the Critique of Pure Reason in Kant’s Collected Works...'

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic terms (foreword, preface, appendix) lowercased and roman
rubrics_metrics.description: Generic terms such as foreword, preface, acknowledgments, introduction, appendix, bibliography, glossary, and index are lowercased and set in roman when used in cross-references or referring to another work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The author states in her preface that...' or 'For further documentation, see the appendix.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbered divisions in text: lowercased words and arabic numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Words denoting parts of long poems or acts and scenes of plays are usually lowercased, neither italicized nor enclosed in quotation marks; numbers are arabic regardless of the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'canto 2', 'stanza 5', 'act 3, scene 2'. Exceptions may be made for cross-references within a work using roman numerals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poems: short poems in quotes, very long works italicized
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of most poems are set in roman type and enclosed in quotation marks. A very long poetic work that constitutes a book is italicized and not enclosed in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poems referred to by first line are capitalized sentence-style, even if first word is lowercased in the original; words capitalized in the original remain capitalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles of plays italicized regardless of length
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of plays, regardless of their length, are italicized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Shaw’s Arms and the Man, in volume 2 of his Plays: Pleasant and Unpleasant'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shorter works like folktales and nursery rhymes set in roman and quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Folktales, fables, fairy tales, nursery rhymes, and the like are usually treated like shorter poems: set in roman type and enclosed in quotation marks. Fairy tales published as books are italicized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '“Aladdin”', 'Ella Enchanted is a retelling by Gail Carson Levine of “Cinderella.”'

rubrics_metrics.name: Pamphlets and reports italicized when freestanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of pamphlets, reports, and similar freestanding publications are, like books, italicized when mentioned or cited in text or notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Young Adult Migration: 2007-2009 to 2010-2012, a report published in 2015...'

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles of forms follow wording and capitalization in the form itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Governmental and other titled or numbered forms can usually be capitalized according to the usage in the form itself; wording should follow the document but may be shortened if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Form 1040-ES, Estimated Tax for Individuals (or 1040-ES)' or 'DHS TRIP Traveler Inquiry Form (or DHS TRIP)'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpublished works: titles in roman and quotes; manuscript collections no quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of unpublished works (theses, dissertations, manuscripts, unpublished transcripts) are set in roman type, capitalized as titles, and enclosed in quotation marks. Titles of manuscript collections take no quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A not-yet-published book under contract may be italicized but must be followed by '(forthcoming)' or equivalent in parentheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Movies, TV, radio, podcast titles italicized; episodes in quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of movies (films) and movie series and of television, radio, and podcast programs and series are italicized. A single episode in a series is set in roman and enclosed in quotation marks. Names of networks and streaming services are set in roman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequels should be numbered as in the source itself; prefer arabic numerals if in doubt. Examples include film titles, series names, episode titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Video games treated like movies (italicized)
rubrics_metrics.description: Video games may be treated like movies and therefore italicized, recognizing narrative/audiovisual similarities; older video games are treated the same. This usage does not apply to other types of games, which are set in roman and capitalized only if trademarked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Pong', 'Tetris', 'Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 3' vs games like 'Monopoly' (roman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Websites and web pages: roman, headline-style, pages/sections in quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of websites mentioned or cited in text are normally set in roman, headline-style, without quotation marks. Titled sections, pages, or special features on a website should be placed in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The title of a website that never had a printed counterpart can be treated like other website titles. Many sites lack formal titles and can be identified by responsible entity plus descriptive phrase or URL (e.g., Apple.com). For citations of online versions of print resources follow relevant rules (see 14.205-10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Blogs and blog posts: blog names italicized, posts in quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of named blogs (and video blogs) can usually be italicized. An initial 'the' can be treated as part of the title in some cases. Titles of blog posts should be placed in quotation marks; untitled posts referred to by date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat blurred distinctions between blogs and websites by default as websites when in doubt. Examples provided for blog title and post usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical works: long works italicized, songs in quotes, instrumental generics not italicized
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of operas, oratorios, tone poems, and other long musical compositions are italicized with standard title capitalization. Titles of songs and shorter compositions are set in roman and enclosed in quotation marks. Generic instrumental work names (symphony, quartet) are capitalized but not italicized; descriptive titles of full works usually italicized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use catalog abbreviations (BWV, K., D.) capitalized; 'op.' is roman and usually lowercased. Recordings: album titles italicized; performers in roman; individual album items treated as songs/sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Works of art and exhibitions: italicize artwork titles; fairs not italicized
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of paintings, drawings, photographs, statues, and other works of art are italicized. Titles of world’s fairs and other large-scale exhibitions are capitalized but not italicized; smaller exhibitions and exhibition catalogs are italicized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Names of works of antiquity often set in roman. Maps known by formal title use italics; maps as illustrations require captions and credit lines (chapter 3).

rubrics_metrics.name: General principle for numerals vs words: spell out zero through one hundred
rubrics_metrics.description: In nontechnical contexts, Chicago's general rule is to spell out whole numbers from zero through one hundred and certain round multiples of those numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This choice is governed by factors including whether the number is large or small, approximation vs exact, entity it stands for, and context. Exceptions and special cases occupy the rest of the chapter; scientific contexts may follow different rules (see Scientific Style and Format).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative rule used by some publications: spell out zero through nine
rubrics_metrics.description: Many publications, especially scientific or journalistic, follow the alternative rule of spelling out only single-digit numbers and using numerals for all others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most exceptions to the general rule also apply to this alternative. Round multiples of hundreds/thousands are typically expressed as numerals under the alternative rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hundreds/thousands with 'hundred' or 'thousand' usually spelled out
rubrics_metrics.description: Whole numbers one through one hundred followed by 'hundred', 'thousand', or 'hundred thousand' are usually spelled out (except in sciences or monetary contexts), whether exact or approximate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'about seven hundred spectators', 'a millennium is a period of one thousand years.' Official counts may use numerals (e.g., attendance 47,122). In contexts with many large numbers prefer numerals for consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbers beginning a sentence always spelled out
rubrics_metrics.description: When a number begins a sentence it is always spelled out; to avoid awkwardness, rephrase the sentence if possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'One hundred ten candidates were accepted' or reword to 'In all, 110 candidates were accepted.' Years that begin sentences should be spelled out or better reworded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out only first of two same-category numbers at sentence start or reword
rubrics_metrics.description: If a number beginning a sentence is followed by another number of the same category, spell out only the first number or reword to avoid multiple spelled-out numbers at the start.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example alternatives are provided to preserve readability and follow rule 9.5.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinals follow the general rule and use 'nd/rd/st' notation
rubrics_metrics.description: The general rule about spelling out numbers applies to ordinals as well as cardinals. Chicago prefers forms like 122nd and 123rd (not 122d/123d). Ordinal letters should not be superscripted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include sports/ranking contexts; italicize 'n' in 'nth degree'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and flexibility when many numbers occur
rubrics_metrics.description: Where many numbers occur within a paragraph or series, maintain consistency in the immediate context; if you must use numerals for one item in a category, use them for all in that category. Exceptions may be made to avoid clustered spelled-out numbers or for a work as a whole if it contains many similar mentions (e.g., ages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In mixed categories items in one category may be numerals and another spelled out; use editorial judgment for readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large numbers and millions/billions: follow general rule with cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Whole numbers combined with million, billion, etc., usually follow the general rule. For fractional quantities in millions or more, use a mixture of numerals and spelled-out numbers for clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that 'billion' and larger terms have different meanings in some countries (long scale vs short scale); editors should query authors unfamiliar with American usage. Examples show mixing (2.3 million; 13.5–14 billion years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Powers of ten and scientific notation for very large/small numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Large round numbers may be expressed in powers of ten (scientific notation); very small numbers may be expressed in negative powers of ten.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and reference to Scientific Style and Format for further details. Use SI prefixes (mega-, giga-, tera-) per SI conventions in appropriate contexts and symbols for units (e.g., MB).
